en: *Siddhaikavīratantra*, Chapter 1 Edited by the Mikkyō Seiten Kyōkai (Nobuo Otsuka) In *Taishō Daigaku Sōgō Bukkyō Kenkyūjo Kiyō* (Journal of the Institute for Comprehensive Buddhist Studies, Taishō University)
% Scanned and typed by Ryugen Tanemura, June 2003. %p.(5)
Oṃ, homage to Mañjughoṣa!
Mañjuvajra, the teacher of the world, proclaimed this tantra for the sake of the world—the Siddhaikavīra, the Lord of Heroes, the most excellent among those who speak. (1)

The deity, indeed, in the form of the mantra, is the bestower of all accomplishments; the practitioner of mantra should meditate upon that very deity, for when that is accomplished, he becomes accomplished. (2)
When the minor accomplishment is achieved by the practitioner whose body has been purified, the great accomplishment arises for one whose body has become a sacred field. (3)
Through this sequence, his attainment of the stages and so forth arises;
like a wish-fulfilling gem, the mantra-practitioner constantly acts for the benefit of sentient beings. (4)
Thinking thus, filled with compassion and questioned by Vajradhara and the others, he spoke for the sake of the world this compendium of perfected mantras. (5)
Oṃ kālumelu kālumelu, paralyze the rain of stones and the rain of snow! Lucca i lucca i svāhā!
This king of mantras, when well-recited, wards off a shower of stones.
Merely by remembering it, or by means of consecrated ashes, one arrests a fall of snow.
Wherever he desires, there he causes [them] to fall;
in this way, he paralyzes lightning, wind, thunderbolts, vajras, and so forth. // 1 //
Oṃ garuḍa haṃsa he he cala cala svāhā!
This king of mantras wards off a shower of stones merely by being remembered.
Having written [the mantra] on a drum with chalk and having empowered a staff [with it], one wards off a shower of stones by the sound of the drum.
In the same way, the sound of a conch and other instruments should also be employed. // 2 //
Oṃ he he! Stay, stay! Bind, bind! Hold fast, hold fast! Restrain, restrain Devadatta, O *ūrṇāmaṇi*! Svāhā!
Having inscribed the name of the enemy together with the mantra upon a palm leaf, one should place it in a crab hole;
this effects the binding of the mouth.
In this way, one likewise paralyzes the sins and other evils of another.
This king of mantras becomes perfected when recited one hundred thousand times according to the ritual for preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*).
Merely by remembering it, one wards off lightning, wind, thunderbolts, vajras, stones, frost, and so forth;
it also arrests heavy rain.
With ash consecrated by this mantra, one binds the mouths of mice, mosquitoes, and the like;
it wards off disturbances from birds, insects, moths, and so forth in gardens or fields.
Having written this mantra on a cloth from a cemetery, one [achieves these results].
Having wrapped it together with its name in *madana* [leaves], one should cast it into a jar in a cremation ground, cover it, and bury it right there;
this arrests conception.
Having extracted [the substance], one should wash it with milk and let it flow away in water;
peace will ensue.

Alternatively, having inscribed [the mantra] on birch bark or cloth using turmeric or yellow orpiment, one should fashion a small figure (*puttalaka*) from anthill clay. Having placed this mantra—encircled by *madana* resin—within its heart, one should fill its mouth with ashes and bury it right there.
In debate, it paralyzes the mouth of the opponent.
In legal proceedings, one should empower the tongue of that very effigy with seven recitations of the mantra and pin it with seven thorns;
thus, the binding of the mouth is accomplished.
Having written [the mantra] on a shallow dish with chalk, filling it with ashes, and enclosing it within a casket, one should bury it;
this paralyzes the mouths of those who speak ill.

Having fashioned a ram from clay rubbed from a potter’s hand, one should insert into its thin heart the [mantra] written on birch bark with turmeric and yellow orpiment, fastened with a yellow thread, and placed within a *madanaka* (a type of amulet) inscribed with saffron and other substances.
It arrests anger and [controls] the mouth.
By wearing the mantra written with saffron and other substances on the neck or the arm, one arrests weapons in battle.
When the King of Mantras, fashioned from the clay of an anthill and placed upon the sole of Gaṇapati’s foot, is buried at a crossroads, it arrests the coming and going [of people].
Placed upon the soles of the feet,
it immobilizes all divine [powers].

The King of Mantras, written on birch bark or cloth and placed within the belly of that very [image], wrapped in *madana* [creeper] and cast into a new jar filled with cold water, [neutralizes] the divine [powers].
It paralyzes:
by tying a knot in the hem of one’s upper garment and recollecting the mantra, it paralyzes thieves and the like on the road;
in the forest, it paralyzes horned and fanged creatures.

By throwing seven clods of earth over which the mantra has been recited into water, one effects the breaking of the fangs of aquatic creatures. Having written the mantra interspersed with the names of the principal men of the enemy army in the center of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), and having written eight *laṃ* syllables outside the double-vajra, one should draw a pair of Maheśvara-maṇḍalas on the exterior. This yantra, adorned with a double-vajra and containing Gaṇapati made of *madana* wood, when buried at the junction of the boundaries of the enemy army, paralyzes the host.

The mantra, encapsulated by the *praṇava* (Oṃ... Svāhā), encircled by a pair of the syllable *ṭha*, adorned with eight instances of the syllable *laṃ*, presided over by the Maheśvara-maṇḍala, and embellished with double-vajras (*viśvavajra*), should be placed inside a Gaṇapati image made from clay from an anthill and cast into a jar from a cremation ground; having been buried in a cremation ground, it paralyzes a hostile army, as does an offering of husks (*tuṣahoma*). In the event of a city fire, one should face the fire, consecrate it with this mantra, and throw seven handfuls of water.
He protects whichever house he desires to protect.
To ward off vomiting, one should bind ashes around the neck.
One should firmly squeeze the tip of the little finger and recite the mantra.
It stops hiccups.
With consecrated ashes, one paralyzes the eyes.

In the event of afflictions such as eruptive boils, having inscribed the *cirikā* [the mantra], if one places it at the door of someone's house, it wards off afflictions such as eruptive boils from that person's house.
A great offering (mahābali) consisting of fish, meat, liquor, fermented grain-porridge, and so forth, should be presented outside the village.

Having prepared a pacificatory fire-pit (śāntikakuṇḍa) in the center of the village, one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with five types of sacrificial fuel-sticks (samidh) made from five varieties of rice, anointed with clarified butter.
This paralyzes all calamities caused by malevolent spirits.
By merely reciting it, one wards off anyone who attempts to give away a village or other property.
By reciting it constantly, one becomes invincible to gods, asuras, humans, and nāgas.

This king of mantras emerged from the circle of hair between the eyebrows at the time of the Blessed One, the venerable Śrīsaṃbuddha’s perfect enlightenment, for the purpose of defeating the four Māras.
Therefore, it is well known as the *ūrṇāmaṇi* (wool-jewel).
Having consecrated a small path or similar object with mantras, one should cast it [therein].
It effects the eradication of snakes. Having empowered chalk with mantras, one should write it upon the wall of a house;
it effects the eradication of snakes.

Alternatively, one may bury a ligature carved with a chisel upon a stone slab at the dwelling of wicked beasts, snakes, in a village, or in a city; it effects the binding of fangs for as long as desired.
Upon its removal, there is release.
Even without being consecrated, this mantra performs all rites.
Having consecrated a path-crossing [stone] and other such items, one should cast them;
this effects the binding of the fangs of all fanged creatures.
In the center of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) marked by a Mahendra-maṇḍala, mantras accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) should be written everywhere.
A stake made of wood from a funeral pyre, consecrated seven times with mantras and hidden within the door-panel, paralyzes the livelihood of all those who subsist by trade;
upon its removal, there is liberation. // 3 //
Oṃ nīhi nicule abhayaṃkari elu velu śila pa ḍa i jahaṃ pelu āgāsapantharate ha attaṃdhari khili mo ḍi them bhi jakāre jā hi ṭhakāre hi ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā.
This king of mantras performs all the previously mentioned rites even without being mastered;
furthermore, whatever other task is intended by the practitioner, it accomplishes all of that.
Without doubt, by means of an oblation of salt and black mustard seeds—or alternatively, an oblation of husks—one causes the enemy army to flee. 4.
Oṃ ambāsimbāka pyāsu jom mo phe ḍa i du pyāsu.
Even if this king of mantras has not been mastered, it wards off all terrors for those who recite it constantly.
By making a forehead mark (*tilaka*) with water consecrated seven times with the vajra-mantra, one deludes all adversaries and pacifies even the enraged.
One who is bound is released from bondage by reciting it constantly.
One who has fallen into calamity obtains fearlessness. // 5 //
Hulu hulu! O you whose tongue is flame, hulu hulu! Wherever you have arisen, hulu hulu, right there let you go back, hulu hulu! Svāhā!
This king of mantras, when recited during times distressed by all kinds of strife, quarrels, disputes, and calamities, brings about peace.
Through an oblation of husks, all-pervading peace occurs.
One should recite the mantra and cast whatever flowers have been obtained into water.
One attains all peace and victory; of this there is no doubt. Even when facing fire during a city conflagration, [one is protected].
Having stood there and empowered seven handfuls [of water] with mantras, one should scatter them;
it provides protection for whichever house one wishes to protect. It extinguishes the fire of that which has been consumed by flames.
In the event of a plague among bipeds and quadrupeds, peace is attained through an oblation of husks. // 6 //
Oṃ, O Lotus One, O Lotus-eyed One, O Lotus-lucky One, flash, flash, flash!
Having smeared this king of mantras with ashes, one should wrap it around [the eyes]; it effects the sealing of the eyes.
By wiping with *oṃ*, one paralyzes the eyes.
Looking at an angry person with the eye consecrated seven times, one pacifies them.
One should wash one's face with water consecrated seven times;
one will become beloved by all people.
By writing the mantra, interspersed with the name, upon a wall with chalk, it pacifies all eye diseases.

Having consecrated both eyes seven times with mantras and remaining alone with a focused mind, when a man's left eye throbs, it announces the accomplishment of the task as intended; if the right eye throbs, it indicates inauspiciousness. //7//
Oṃ, O liberator, liberate! O deliverer, deliver! O giver of life and boons, svāhā!
By applying anointed oil to the womb, a pregnant woman gives birth with ease.
Having become facing toward one who is bound, one should cast seven handfuls of consecrated water at the three junctions of the day; thus, the bound person is released from bondage.
Having written [the mantra] on birch bark with saffron or yellow orpiment and binding it to the head, one releases someone from bondage. // 8 //
Oṃ! O Harimarkaṭa, you who possess a thousand arms, release Devadatta from his bonds! Svāhā!
Having consecrated chalk and drawn [the mantra] upon the surface of the ground, one should repeatedly erase it again and again in reverse order;
thus, one who is bound is liberated from bondage.
Or, having written the mantra on a birch-bark leaf and wearing it upon the head, one who is bound is released from bondage. // 9 //
Oṃ, O Savior, save us; O Liberator, liberate us; O Deliverer, deliver us; O Bestower of Life and Boons, svāhā!

This king of mantras, when well-recited, accomplishes all rites. If one anoints the womb with oil consecrated seven times, a pregnant woman will give birth easily. Having drunk three mouthfuls of water consecrated seven times, a woman with a hidden fetus will give birth easily.
By reciting [this] constantly, one liberates oneself or another from bondage;
by wearing a leaf-inscription on the neck or the arm, one is released from bondage. // 10 //
Oṃ tāre tu tāre ture, liberate [me], O giver of life and boons, svāhā!
This king of mantras performs all the previously mentioned rites with saffron.

Having written the mantra interspersed with the name of a person on birch bark and encircled it with the *madana* plant, one should place it inside a new jar filled with fragrant water and worship it with fragrant flowers and other offerings at the three junctions of the day; for him, there will be victory in all quarrels, disputes, and legal contests. // 11 //
[Oṃ] In a forest of castor-oil trees, a crow has arrived at the bank of the Gaṅgā; let the messenger drink the water, and let the pregnant woman be free from her pains. [Svāhā].
One should have the messenger who has arrived drink three mouthfuls of water consecrated seven times; the pregnant woman will give birth easily. // 12 //
Oṃ amariṇi jīvantīye svāhā!
This king of mantras, when well-recited, performs all rites. By drinking water consecrated with this mantra, eruptive boils do not occur.
For wounds caused by malignant spiders, *markaṭikā* insects, erysipelas, and the like, one should recite over turmeric, *harītakī*, *kuṣṭha*, and other such substances and apply them as an ointment.
He becomes healthy;
in the event of all diseases and afflictions, he becomes healthy by means of binding a *gaṇḍaka* [amulet].
By reciting it constantly, one whose life has reached its end becomes long-lived for a hundred years;
by performing a fire-oblation of sesame seeds and ghee, one brings about peace in all circumstances.
By drinking consecrated medicine,
one is liberated from all diseases.
Having prepared "centipede-washed ghee" with this mantra, one should smear it upon the affected limb.
One becomes healthy.
In the case of a headache, by consecrating oil with mantras and massaging the head with it, one becomes healthy.
In the case of malignant ulcers, one should cover them with water [consecrated by mantras].
The patient becomes healthy.
In the case of splenic enlargement (*plīhodara*), one should cut it with a *vārttāku* knife;
the spleen is then severed.

Having combined the roots of *nirguṇḍī* and *nimba* with a peacock’s feather in one place and consecrated them one hundred and eight times, one should offer incense; this destroys fevers such as those recurring every day, every two days, every three days, or every four days.
It also destroys *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *brahmarākṣasas*, and the like.
For women whose children have died, by bathing them with a jar consecrated one hundred and eight times, their children become living.
By writing the mantra on birch bark and wearing it on the waist or the arm, protection for the fetus is secured.
By recollecting the mantra in battle, one attains victory.
Through sprinkling with water consecrated by the mantra, one removes all diseases. (13)
Oṃ, svāhā to the movement of the feet!
This king of mantras, when well-accomplished through the ritual of prior service (*pūrvasevā*), performs all activities.
In the event of the fear of eruptive boils (*visphoṭaka*), by drinking water consecrated with this mantra, no eruptive boils shall arise.
By writing out this leaf-mantra and placing it at the door, no eruptions will occur.
Against all calamities, this great protection [is achieved] by performing a fire-oblation (*homa*) of sesame seeds smeared with clarified butter.
Having taken a crow’s wing-feather in one's hand and recited the mantra ten thousand times, if one casts it onto the roof of someone's house, that person is driven away. 14.
Oṃ piśāci parṇaśabari, destroyer of all calamities, svāhā!
This great vidyā destroys all calamities for bipeds and quadrupeds;
even if not yet accomplished, it performs all rites.
Through fire-offerings (homa), recitation (jāpa), meditation (dhyāna), or by means of a medicinal pill, or by drinking water consecrated with mantras or by wiping [with it], it removes diseases.
Having written the mantra on birch bark with saffron and wearing it on the neck or the arm, one attains victory in legal disputes;
one is liberated from quartan fever and other irregular fevers;
and it removes the fear of *rākṣasa*s and other such beings.
In times of strife, quarrel, and dispute, one attains victory;
one becomes invulnerable to tigers, crocodiles, great serpents, thieves, and the like;
and through constant recitation, one becomes beloved by all people. // 15 //
Oṃ adva tṛtīyā, paralyze the eye of [Name], ṭhaḥ ṭhaḥ svāhā!
On whichever lunar day one's eye throbs, that day should be marked with chalk on a wall or a wooden board.
By means of the letter *ṭha*, one should form a triple fold; this pacifies eye pain. // 16 //
Oṃ Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa hūṃ phaṭ!
This king of mantras, when recited even once, burns away all sins;
it brings protection in every situation;
and by striking with beans and other such items, it removes the fear of malevolent spirits and the like.
Having drawn [the design] with chalk on a shallow bowl, one should hang it at the door;
this provides protection for infants who have recently been born.

Having fashioned a doll out of *madana* wood measuring four finger-breadths in height, one should write the mantra together with the name of the person to be influenced upon its heart and insert it there.
One should pin her mouth with a thorn; thus the mouth of the opponent in debate becomes pinned.
One should pin her feet; this paralyzes her movement. One should pin her heart; this paralyzes her anger.
If one takes the name [of the person] and drives in a stake made of human shank-bone or iron into whichever limbs [he desires], those limbs of his perish.
If one buries it at the gate of an enemy, one causes him to be driven away.
By throwing consecrated ashes from a cremation ground onto the door-panel, one causes him to be driven away.
Having consecrated a sword with mantras, one who enters into battle attains victory;
in whatever undertaking [one undertakes].
When [the deity] has arisen, one should offer a bali-oblation; that succeeds.
Whatever the mantra-practitioner desires, whether auspicious or inauspicious, all that he accomplishes by mere recitation. // 17 //
Oṃ! Flow in the kāśa grass, flow in the kuśa grass; flow, you, into my empty dwelling, just as you flow for the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, svāhā!
When it is flowing, by wiping the eyes, peace is attained. // 18 //
Oṃ jambhe mohe hṛdayahṛdayāvartani hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!

By means of this king of mantras, if one washes one’s face at the time of dawn with water consecrated seven times while reciting it during the *ākāra-rudita* [the sound of weeping], one becomes beloved by all people.

Having taken collyrium from the eyes of a cow using a white lotus fiber and cow’s ghee under the asterism of Puṣya, one should consecrate it eight hundred times; with eyes anointed by that, one becomes enchanting to all women.
One should combine the root of the *adhaḥpuṣpikā* plant with sandalwood (*śrīkhaṇḍa*) together under the asterism of Puṣya.
One should apply a forehead mark (tilaka) consecrated one hundred and eight times with this; by it, even an angry lord becomes gracious.
One becomes victorious in quarrels, strife, and disputes.
By constantly reciting it according to the rules before [the deity], one causes agitation. 19.
Oṃ, O Paralyzer, paralyze! O Crusher, crush! O Deluder, delude! O Protector, protect me, O Giver of Boons, O Siddhalocanā! Svāhā!
The heart-mantra of Locanā dispels all fear.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Siddhaikavīra-mahātantrarāja*.
